entities.name: Abû 'Umar ibn Sa'îd
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abû ‘Umar ibn Sa’îd, whose full name was Abû ‘Umar ibn Sa’îd ibn Hakam al Qurashi, served as the last independent *ra’îs* (ruler) of Manûrqa (Menorca) from 1282 until his death in 1287. His brief reign marked the definitive end of autonomous Muslim governance in the Balearic Islands, a process initiated by the Aragonese conquest of Majorca in 1229. As the final sovereign of the Taifa of Manûrqa, Abû ‘Umar’s fate became inextricably linked with the relentless expansion of the Crown of Aragon into the western Mediterranean, concluding centuries of Islamic political presence on the archipelago.

His rule was dominated by the looming threat of the Aragonese *Reconquista*. In 1285, King Alfonso III of Aragon, driven by strategic ambition and a desire to consolidate Aragonese control over the Balearics, launched a formidable invasion fleet against Manûrqa. Abû ‘Umar, facing overwhelming military might, resisted valiantly but was ultimately forced to surrender. On January 21, 1287, he signed the Treaty of Sant Lluís, a capitulation agreement that effectively ended the Taifa of Manûrqa. This treaty granted Abû ‘Umar and a small retinue safe passage to North Africa, allowing him to take his personal library and a limited number of followers, though the vast majority of the island's Muslim inhabitants faced enslavement or expulsion.
